Newborn Care

Choosing contraception while breastfeeding

Updated: October 5, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Breastfeeding does not automatically prevent another pregnancy. Ovulation can return before the first period, so waiting for bleeding to restart can leave a gap in protection. Several contraceptive methods can be used while breastfeeding, including long-acting devices, progestin-only options and condoms. The best fit depends on your health, how recently you gave birth, feeding circumstances and when you might want another pregnancy.

Plan before fertility becomes obvious

Pregnancy can become possible from about three weeks after birth, even if you are breastfeeding and have not had a period. The first ovulation may happen before any menstrual warning. If you do not want another pregnancy, discuss a method before resuming vaginal sex.

You can make that plan during pregnancy, before leaving the birth setting or at a later appointment. Some methods can start immediately after delivery; others need different timing. There is no universal requirement to wait for the six-week check.

Sex should resume when you feel ready and recovery allows. If there were complications, stitches or ongoing pain, ask your maternity team for individual advice. Contraception does not remove the need for comfort, consent and recovery.

When breastfeeding can work as contraception

The lactational amenorrhoea method, or LAM, relies on breastfeeding suppressing ovulation. All three conditions need to apply: your baby is under six months old, periods have not returned, and breastfeeding is exclusive or nearly exclusive with frequent feeds day and night.

Guidance commonly specifies no gap longer than four hours during the day or six hours at night. Regular formula or solid feeds, longer sleep stretches, fewer feeds or the return of periods can mean that LAM no longer provides the expected protection.

Expressing milk may not suppress ovulation in the same way as frequent direct feeding, and evidence about pumping-based LAM is limited. If you mainly pump, supplement feeds or are unsure whether the criteria apply, arrange another method.

LAM is a temporary method with specific rules, not a promise that any amount of breastfeeding prevents pregnancy. Have a transition plan before six months or an earlier feeding change. It does not protect against sexually transmitted infections.

Compare effectiveness using the same kind of measure

Perfect use means following every instruction consistently. Typical use includes real-life missed pills, late injections and condom errors. Contraceptive percentages generally describe a year of use, not the chance of pregnancy from one sexual encounter.

US CDC estimates put typical-use pregnancy rates below 1 in 100 users per year for IUDs and implants, around 4 in 100 for the injection, 7 in 100 for pills and 13 in 100 for external condoms. Estimates vary between studies and health systems. LAM is assessed over its first-six-month period, so it should not be compared as though it were a year-long method.

Effectiveness is only one consideration. Bleeding patterns, daily effort, comfort with a procedure, access, medical eligibility, STI protection and future pregnancy plans also matter.

Hormonal and copper IUDs

An intrauterine device, or IUD, is a small device placed inside the uterus by a trained clinician. Both copper and hormonal types are long-acting and reversible, and both can be suitable while breastfeeding.

Hormonal IUDs release levonorgestrel, a progestin. One important effect is thickening cervical mucus so sperm are less able to pass through. Periods often become lighter, and some users stop having menstrual bleeding. A copper IUD contains no contraceptive hormone and affects sperm function; it may make periods heavier or more crampy.

Current US contraceptive approvals differ by product: Mirena and Liletta can be used for up to eight years, Kyleena for five years and Skyla for three years. These durations refer to pregnancy prevention; use for another indication may have a different limit. Confirm the device, local approval and replacement date with the service that fits it.

You can ask to have an IUD removed whenever you want. Fertility can return promptly afterward, although no method can guarantee how quickly a particular person will conceive. If you are switching methods, arrange coverage before removal rather than leaving an unintended gap.

IUD insertion after birth: timing and risks

An IUD can sometimes be fitted immediately after delivery by a trained team. UK guidance describes fitting within 48 hours of birth or, if that window is missed, usually from four weeks onward. Local services and clinical guidance may offer different postpartum arrangements.

Immediate postpartum insertion has a higher chance of the device being expelled than insertion later. That needs discussion and follow-up, but it is not the same as saying that all early insertion causes infection. An active postpartum uterine infection is a reason not to insert an IUD at that time.

Having more than one sexual partner does not automatically make an IUD unsuitable. The relevant questions are STI risk, screening and whether an infection is currently present. Screening for gonorrhoea or chlamydia can often be performed at the insertion visit; known current infection or purulent cervicitis requires appropriate management before insertion.

Discuss pain relief before the procedure. Cramping and spotting can occur afterward, and bleeding patterns may change over the first months. Heavy or persistent bleeding, fever, worsening pelvic pain or possible expulsion need assessment. The rare risk of uterine perforation is also part of informed counselling, particularly around postpartum insertion.

An IUD does not prevent STIs. Condoms can be used alongside it when STI protection is needed.

The progestin-only pill, or mini pill

The mini pill contains a progestin without estrogen and is a common option while breastfeeding. It may be available by prescription or over the counter depending on the formulation and country.

Current guidance allows progestin-only pills to start immediately after birth when medically appropriate. You do not routinely need to wait six to eight weeks. Whether backup contraception is needed depends on the particular pill, time since birth and whether all LAM criteria are met.

Take your pill according to its instructions each day. Some formulations have a short late-pill window, while others allow more time. Not every pack contains 28 active hormone tablets; some include inactive tablets. Do not apply another person’s schedule or missed-pill advice to your own product.

Bleeding may become irregular, lighter, more frequent or absent. No monthly bleed is guaranteed, and having no bleed does not automatically mean pregnancy. If pills were missed or symptoms suggest pregnancy, follow testing advice.

Some users report headaches, mood or libido changes, although an individual symptom may have other causes. Functional ovarian cysts can occur and often settle on their own. Report persistent or significant symptoms rather than assuming they are something you must tolerate.

Fertility generally returns quickly after stopping the pill. There is no routine requirement to wait several months before trying for pregnancy, but a preconception discussion can help you plan medicines and supplements.

Will hormonal contraception reduce milk supply?

Estrogen-containing contraception can reduce milk production in some people, particularly while feeding is being established. Progestin-only methods are generally compatible with breastfeeding; available studies have not shown consistent adverse effects on feeding or infant growth, although evidence has limitations.

It is therefore misleading to say that every hormonal method commonly reduces milk. If you notice a change after starting a method, consider it alongside feeding frequency, milk transfer, illness and other factors with a clinician or lactation professional.

More frequent effective milk removal can be part of an individualized supply plan, but routinely pumping after every feed is not necessary simply because you start a mini pill. It can add a substantial burden and should have a clear purpose.

Get feeding support if your baby is not feeding well, has fewer wet nappies than expected or is not gaining weight adequately. If you want to change contraception, arrange another method so that addressing a feeding concern does not create an unplanned gap.

Condoms: hormone-free protection and STI prevention

External condoms keep semen from entering the vagina. They contain no contraceptive hormones, do not reduce milk supply and can be used whenever you resume sex. They are widely available without a prescription.

Correct use means a new condom for every encounter, put on before genital contact and used through withdrawal. Check the packet and expiry date, open it carefully and use a compatible lubricant. Dryness during breastfeeding may make lubrication particularly helpful.

Condoms are up to about 98% effective with consistent correct use; typical-use protection is lower because they may be applied late, slip, split or be forgotten. A condom can be combined with an IUD, implant or pill for additional pregnancy protection.

Latex and suitable synthetic condoms also reduce the risk of many STIs, although they cannot eliminate every risk, particularly from uncovered skin. Natural-membrane condoms are not a dependable choice for STI prevention.

Do not use two condoms at once or an external and internal condom together. Additional spermicide is not needed for ordinary condom use and is not a substitute for correct use. If a condom breaks or slips, seek timely advice about emergency contraception and any STI exposure.

The contraceptive implant

An implant is a small flexible rod placed under the skin of the upper arm. Nexplanon contains etonogestrel, a progestin that suppresses ovulation and thickens cervical mucus. It is highly effective and does not require a daily action.

The US Nexplanon approval was extended to up to five years in 2026. Duration and available implant products vary by country, so use the replacement date given for your actual device. Nexplanon is not the only implant available worldwide.

An implant can be placed immediately after birth when appropriate, including during breastfeeding. A trained professional inserts and removes it. You can request removal sooner, and fertility may return quickly afterward.

Irregular bleeding is common and may be unpredictable. Contact the service for persistent arm pain, redness or swelling, fever or chills, unusually heavy vaginal bleeding, or if you cannot feel the implant where you were shown. These findings need assessment rather than a promise that complications never occur.

The contraceptive injection

Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, or DMPA, is a progestin injection sold under names such as Depo-Provera. Standard repeat dosing is about every three months; CDC guidance specifies 13 weeks. Other injectable products can have different schedules.

The injection can be used while breastfeeding, including soon after birth when clinically appropriate. Personal risk factors and local guidance determine timing. Keep a record of the next due date, because protection cannot be assumed indefinitely after a missed appointment.

If you are late, contact the service promptly. Whether you need a pregnancy assessment, backup protection or emergency contraception depends on how late the dose is and recent sex. Do not guess from the phrase three months.

Possible effects include irregular or absent periods, weight gain, headache and abdominal discomfort. DMPA can reduce bone mineral density during use; the balance of benefits and risks and ongoing suitability should be reviewed with a clinician.

Unlike a pill that can be stopped or a device that can be removed, an injection continues working after it has been given. Return of fertility can take months after the last dose and sometimes more than a year. This delay is variable and does not mean permanent infertility, but it matters if another pregnancy is wanted soon.

What about the combined pill, patch or ring?

Combined hormonal methods contain estrogen as well as a progestin. Estrogen is relevant both to milk supply and to the increased blood-clot risk soon after birth.

They are not suitable immediately postpartum. For example, UK guidance usually advises breastfeeding parents to wait at least six weeks before considering them. A clinician must still assess clot risk, medical history and feeding circumstances; reaching six weeks does not automatically make every combined method suitable.

It is also too broad to say that estrogen must be avoided for the entire time you breastfeed. Some people can use a combined method later after discussing its risks, benefits and alternatives. Choose the timing with your clinician rather than relying on a general article.

Emergency contraception while breastfeeding

If a condom breaks, pills are missed or sex happens without adequate contraception, contact a pharmacist or sexual health service promptly. Emergency contraception is time-sensitive. You do not need to wait for a period or prove that pregnancy is likely before asking.

The main options are a copper IUD, levonorgestrel emergency pills and ulipristal acetate. Ulipristal acts on progesterone receptors and is not simply another progestin-only mini pill. Older combined estrogen–progestin emergency regimens are less effective and cause more nausea than the dedicated pill options.

Oral emergency contraception should be taken as soon as possible, within the relevant product and clinical window. Ulipristal can be used up to five days after sex; levonorgestrel works best earlier and becomes less effective with delay. A copper IUD is the most effective option and may provide ongoing contraception if suitable.

NHS specialist breastfeeding guidance allows oral emergency contraception from day 21 after birth and a copper IUD for this purpose from day 28. It prefers copper or levonorgestrel when suitable, while allowing ulipristal after assessment. These postpartum thresholds are separate from the time limit after sex.

For a full-term, healthy infant, that specialist guidance does not require breastfeeding interruption after a single dose of levonorgestrel or ulipristal. Evidence is more limited for ulipristal; ask for individualized advice if your baby is premature or unwell, or if local product instructions differ.

Ask when to restart your usual contraception. After ulipristal, hormonal contraception is generally delayed for at least five days because taking it too soon can reduce the emergency pill’s effect. After levonorgestrel it can usually restart immediately. Use backup protection as directed and follow pregnancy-testing advice.

An emergency pill does not provide reliable protection for later sex in the same cycle. It is useful when needed, while an ongoing method provides more dependable routine coverage. Access, cost and prescription rules vary locally.

Choose a method that fits your life

A daily pill may suit someone who wants to avoid a procedure and can remember it consistently. An IUD or implant may fit someone who wants longer protection with little daily effort. Condoms offer hormone-free use and STI protection, while an injection avoids daily dosing but may delay return to fertility.

Tell the clinician about your feeding pattern, medical conditions, medicines, bleeding preferences and future pregnancy plans. Ask how soon the method works, what backup is needed, which symptoms require help and how to stop or change it.

There is no single best method for every breastfeeding parent. A good plan is one you understand, can access and want to use, with a clear way to review it when your circumstances change.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

CDC and NHS guidance allow several methods to start immediately postpartum, while estrogen-containing methods require more careful timing and assessment. LAM works only while its age, menstrual and feeding criteria remain satisfied.

Current product information updates the contraceptive duration of several devices. NHS specialist guidance distinguishes emergency contraception choices and breastfeeding advice, including the need for individual advice for a premature or unwell infant.

How BeMama can help

Keep your method name, start date and replacement or injection date with your care notes. BeMama can help you prepare questions about feeding, side effects and future pregnancy plans; a clinician or pharmacist should confirm the method and backup instructions.

When to seek help

Seek prompt advice for severe pelvic pain, fever after device insertion, unusually heavy bleeding, a suspected expelled IUD or a problem at the implant site. If contraception may have failed, ask about emergency contraception without waiting for symptoms.

Evidence notes updated: October 5, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Ovulation may return before your first period.
  • Breastfeeding alone is not reliable unless all LAM criteria apply.
  • IUDs, implants and progestin-only options can be suitable during breastfeeding.
  • Check the exact product and current local duration or dosing schedule.
  • Condoms add STI protection that most contraceptives do not provide.
  • Emergency contraception is available during breastfeeding; act promptly.

Frequently asked questions

Can I get pregnant before my first period after birth?

Yes. Ovulation can occur first, and pregnancy can become possible from about three weeks postpartum. Plan contraception before relying on bleeding as a warning.

Does pumping count the same as direct breastfeeding for LAM?

That is uncertain. Expressing may not suppress ovulation in the same way. If you mainly pump or do not meet all LAM criteria, choose another contraceptive method.

Must I wait six weeks to start the mini pill?

Not routinely. Progestin-only pills can usually start immediately after birth when medically appropriate. Backup requirements depend on the pill and circumstances.

Does every hormonal method reduce milk supply?

No. Progestin-only methods are generally compatible with breastfeeding. If supply or infant growth is concerning, seek an individualized feeding and contraception review.

How long do hormonal IUDs last?

Current US contraceptive approvals are up to eight years for Mirena and Liletta, five for Kyleena and three for Skyla. Confirm your product, indication and local replacement date.

How long does Nexplanon last?

The US approval was extended to five years in 2026. Follow the current advice for the actual product and country where you receive it.

Which method may delay return to fertility?

The DMPA injection can delay fertility for months after the last dose and sometimes over a year. Fertility generally returns more quickly after stopping pills or removing an IUD or implant.

Do emergency pills always mean stopping breastfeeding?

No. Current NHS specialist guidance does not require an interruption after a single levonorgestrel or ulipristal dose for a full-term, healthy infant. Ask about premature or unwell infants and your local instructions.

Can I restart the mini pill immediately after ulipristal?

Usually you should wait at least five days before restarting hormonal contraception, then use backup as advised. Ask the pharmacist for instructions specific to your method.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
